title: A History of Future Cities
author: Daniel Brook
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Comparative urban history of St. Petersburg, Shanghai, Mumbai and Dubai, not narrow architectural appreciation or technical planning instruction. Urban history and political power are central, so both thematic deductions apply. Cross-period comparison reaches the contemporary world; no single closed historical endpoint. The causal claim that commercial openness creates political change is suggestive rather than established. No high-confidence foundational veto established by inspected reviews. Not selected on expert consensus: a specialist review was located but its substantive assessment was inaccessible.
notes: Reported cases and notes support descriptive history; the causal generalization from four selected cities is less secure.
Connects trade, imposed modernization, architecture, migration and political institutions.
Useful comparisons of imported models and unintended institutional change, with limited predictive reliability.
Explains tensions between commercial openness and centralized control; alternative causes receive less attention.

D=7, moderate confidence from Kirkus, Publishers Weekly and reader reports. Four cases add contrasting institutional histories; extended local narrative has lower yield for this reader. No full-text density audit.
Historical comparisons endure, while predictions about future political opening remain uncertain.
Trade and infrastructure fit partly, but the emphasis is urban and cultural history.
Experienced journalist; specialist review exists but its findings were not inspected.
Four-city comparison provides an accessible recurring structure.
Vivid prose with some broad East-West categories.

title: The Retreat of Western Liberalism
author: Edward Luce
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Analysis of Western institutions and economic discontent, not a campaign manual; criticism of political leaders does not by itself establish V6. The inspected Australian Foreign Affairs review praises diagnosis but identifies weak prioritization, simplified intellectual history and moral exhortation. These lower evidence and mechanism assessments; they do not establish a high-confidence foundational veto. Western comparative scope and global consequences prevent a US-only thematic deduction; political institutions are central, T12=-10. Contemporary diagnosis is treated as a 2017 argument, not a verified current forecast. Not selected for the praised-book group because specialist reception is mixed.
notes: Reporting supports the diagnosis; broad causal claims and simplified accounts of thinkers limit confidence.
Links economic insecurity, inequality, elite incentives and democratic institutions across countries.
Useful institutional warning signs, with limited operational guidance or prioritization.
Several plausible causal pathways are described but not separated by strong comparative tests.

D=7, moderate confidence from the Australian Foreign Affairs review, Publishers Weekly and reader reports. The short synthesis covers distinct institutional stresses; familiar crisis lists and exhortation reduce yield.
Institutional tensions endure, but the argument is closely tied to the 2016 political moment.
Institutional power and strategic risk fit partly; technology and production are secondary.
Experienced international correspondent; substantive review criticism remains relevant.
Concise essay structure makes the argument accessible.
Forceful and readable, with occasional rhetorical simplification.

title: The Elements of Moral Philosophy
author: James Rachels; later editions revised by Stuart Rachels
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. General moral argument in plain language, not specialist technical proficiency or formal proof training. A textbook label alone does not establish H3's technical exclusion. Religion is one limited chapter within a broad ethics survey, so V8 does not apply to the central purpose. Philosophy is central, T12=-10. Competing ethical theories are explained and challenged; the existence of philosophical disagreement alone is not a V9 veto on an introductory comparative account. Reader reception is mixed, so this is not selected as highly praised by readers.
notes: Makes arguments and objections explicit; introductory simplifications and author preferences remain visible.
Compares ethical frameworks but offers little integration of technological or economic systems.
Useful distinctions for evaluating duties, consequences and consistency across cases.
Argumentative structure is developed, but empirical institutional mechanisms are peripheral.

D=7, moderate confidence from publisher contents and detailed reader reports. Distinct theories and contrasting cases add learning; elementary treatment limits yield for an experienced reader. The large hosted PDF could not be retrieved for a direct text audit.
Core ethical questions and counterarguments are durable.
Pragmatic reasoning fits partly; preferred technical and industrial domains are largely absent.
Established moral philosophers and long-standing academic use, without treating adoption as proof of every argument.
Self-contained chapters and concrete cases support clear exposition.
Generally precise and economical prose; simplified formulations need context.

title: The World After Capital
author: Albert Wenger
vetoReason: The central transition thesis assumes sufficient physical capital and that reallocating attention can sustain a knowledge economy. Economist Luigi Zingales and financial journalist Bethany McLean directly challenge the adequacy, distribution and incentive premises, not merely details. Their discussion also considers Wenger's defense and supports some platform proposals. These unresolved foundational assumptions meet V9 despite useful subsidiary ideas.
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Published paperback exists, so H1 does not apply to the earlier online draft. Earliest public book draft was being read by May 2016; original-production year uses 2016 with moderate confidence, not the 2021 print date. Political economy and philosophy are central, T12=-10. Neither reform advocacy nor humanism establishes ideological extremism. Meditation is subsidiary, not the dominant purpose. V9 concerns the core scarcity transition; counterfactual scoring retains both criticism and the practical value of platform interoperability proposals.
notes: Citations and illustrative calculations are present, but the core sufficiency and behavioral claims remain weakly established.
Connects digital technology, capital, attention, knowledge and institutions, with overcompressed transitions.
Interoperability and user-controlled filtering are concrete reusable proposals; broader allocation prescriptions are less secure.
Some platform incentives are explained; the transition from aggregate sufficiency to effective allocation is incomplete.

D=6, moderate confidence from the author overview, references, extended author interview and reader reports. Several distinct proposals add learning; compressed assertions leave important intermediate reasoning unstated. Reader reports include earlier drafts.
Attention scarcity is durable; confident stage-of-history framing and technology expectations may age poorly.
Computing, knowledge production and resource allocation fit strongly.
Relevant venture and computing experience; substantive economist criticism limits authority for the broad social thesis.
The scarcity sequence is easy to follow but conceals unresolved transitions.
Accessible wording, with categorical claims broader than the evidence.
